Author: @solid-kong
Content: So to clarify about game key cards, the way they work is that you put the cartridge in the game slot of the system, it then downloads the game from the eshop, and then the cartridge works as a license that allows you to play the game with no further online check ins, ever. You can resell it, and then someone else can do the same process. It's basically a physical digital game that allows you to resell the digital game or lend it to a friend. It's weird but not exactly the same thing that was happening on Switch 1 with incomplete game cards that required a download to access the full game or the boxes that came empty with no game card inside. It's basically a way to allow 3rd parties to spend less on the cartridges. It's odd, but at least it has resale value in theory as long as Nintendo's servers exist, which, according to theme, the same eshop and accounts that were introduced with the Switch 1 in 2017 will keep being used going into the future.

Author: @NightDragon2383
Content:
To the people saying "Well games were $70 back in the 90s", yeah there was a reason for that, for example it cost like $25-$30 a pop to manufacture N64 games in some cases around the console's launch, plus with Nintendo's expensive licensing fees that they charged for 3rd parties, most 3rd party N64 games needed to be priced at $70-$75 at retail to be profitable.

But as time went on, prices went DOWN... by 1998, most new N64 games cost $49.99 at retail to be in line with the PS1, which had most of its new games retailing at the $39.99 - $49.99 price point by this time.  This pricing carried over to the PS2/GC/XB generation, with most new games being $50 across the board and in some cases even cheaper despite the increased development costs.  Then the "HD" consoles forced an increased back up to $60 for most new games justified by increasing dev costs, but this has traditionally been the ceiling that the average game was priced at for generations now.

Asking people to suddenly pay $70-$80 for a piece of software that in many cases isn't even offered in a physical format anymore is just a bridge too far.

Piracy is almost unbeatable; Price: free, ads minimal if not absent. Mods: available, most games, especially console games do not have mods. FREE mods: the games that do have/allow mods are pretty wide and varied, a minority in this case, but the amount of games that charge real cash for 'mods' in games is not insignificant. Respect: I hesitated to add this here, but it's true, I do not want to pirate a game from a studio I respect. I want them to be paid and looked after. Alternatively, I have zero respect for studios that do not, in turn, respect me as a customer.

If you treat me as the enemy, as someone whose money you 'do not need or want', then you won't get my business, my money, or even my attention. Author: @skulltula6799
Content: This is what happens when you go to a fiat currency. Fun fact, price for a house in 1950 in gold ozs ( which our dollar was an equivalent of gold at the time) was 211 Ozs. In 2024, the average cost for a house in gold was 206 Ozs of gold (while having increased in size from 1000 sq ft to 1500 sq ft). Things aren't getting more expensive in terms of purchasing power, we're just being paid in diluted currency. There is of course elements of greed, but the real culprit is fiat currency. In the constitution the only recognized legal tender is gold/silver coins, and fed gov was only granted the ability to "coin" new tender (gold/silver coins). That was twisted to mean that the government could print legal fiat tender, to fund constant deficits. The founding father's were well aware of the dangers of "paper currency" due to having printed out so many worthless bills to fund the continental army, and so engraved against it in the constitution. I don't think literal gold/silver coins would work in the digital age, but we need to get back to a commodity backed currency.

One thing I don't see many people talking about is the fact that some reason the switch 2 only has Wi-Fi 6 support? If I'm going to pay $450 for a console that's themed around multiplayer then I want Wi-Fi 7.  Nintendo uses P2P protocol for most of their games meaning they rarely host online servers and instead one player acts as the server and they rest connect to them directly.  This is why the switch one had some really bad networking problems. Without Wi-Fi 7, if you want to play online, you're almost always going to need to be connected to a hard line.

It's a pirate's life for me, in fact I'm probably going to contribute to the emulator.  Also, what's the point of having 120hz when the game console will likely not be able to use it? The steam deck is 720p and most of its games run pretty well around 40 to 45 FPS.  But a higher frame rate means lower battery life, and if the leaks are to be believed, the hardware of the switch to is very similar to the steam deck in terms of processing power.  From a thermodynamics point of view, you just can't make a GPU and CPU that's small enough which would be efficient enough to run these games at those frame rates while also having a reasonable battery life.

Author: @ThatGuyNamedRick
Content:
Games costed 40, 50 USD in the late 80's to early 90's due to the format (cartridges), quite literally, needing to be manufactured (unlike discs that could be printed at a fraction of the cost). Game boxes at that time also had manuals, cloth maps, figurines, and cloth patches you can sew or iron on your backpack and jackets, things had VALUE. Back in the 90's when you saw that "Nintendo Seal of Quality" or "Sega Approved" you rested assured that every game was COMPLETE, with minimal bugs, and worth your time and money to play. Now we're seeing digital goods, with half the content, with the fraction of the quality, being piecemealed, re-released and sold back to us at the approval of investors and stakeholders willing to kill ideas if it doesn't make an ungodly sum of money. Look around you, when was the last time you heard "X game is sleeper, a cult classic." on any AAA game the past decade and a half? I sure haven't.

Minimally Viable Products should be placed at minimal cost. At this point, most games aren't even WORTH pirating in the first place.

Author: @Darkbeast42
Content:
I'm just a layman, but this just seems like a terrible business decision. At $60 I'm willing to take a gambal on a game that I'm not entirely sure I'm going to like, so I wind up buying a lot of games. At $70-$80 I'm only going to get games I know I'll like/love. The only Nintendo franchises I'm willing to shell out that kind of cash for are Smash, Xenoblade, and maybe Fire Emblem and Zelda. All of this is to say that I would be purchasing a Switch 2 for maybe 5 games. I can't justify that kind of investment.

If they kept their prices low, they would make less money on each purchase but would sell enough games to make up for it. Then you'd have a larger audience you can sell sequels and merch to. 

Maybe I'm wrong, I'm not a business analyst or anything, but I just think its smarter to sell $60 games to 10K people than to sell $80 games to 6K people.

Author: @MrKsan05
Content:
I'm a old man now (57) My first game system was the O.G. Pong, then I went to the Atari and then Commadore 64, I've been gaming my whole life, I LOVE games. Back then games cost from $40 to $50 and this was 1970's and 1980's so games stayed at $50 for most of my life. I can see games needing to go up some but I've watched programs saying they would be $100 to $150 by 2026. I'm just not going to pay that and I draw my line around $65 to maybe $70 for top AAA games.

 Everything around us has been going up higher and higher in price but games some how stayed $50 or close to it for 50 years? Thats pretty incredible, they had to go up in price at some point, look at what games are now, and what it takes to make them compaired to just little blocks in (My) old days. I was born a Diabetic, and was always very sick growing up, I think that's why my parents bought me gaming systems. I couldn't keep up in sports.....

  I had to go to a diabetic doctor in a big city every 4 months. When we would leave the doctors office my mother would take me to Sears in the big mall, I was so excited as we would ride the escalator up to the top floor and as we would get close to the top of the escalator you could see the game case with the games. My mother would buy me one game every 4 months if my diabetes was good at the doctor (Me not cheating on eating) I remember even way back then, my mom saying $50 is to much for a game, but she would buy it because she loved me. There were no game reviews back then, so I had to do my best to pick out a good game, I would ask the salesmen about the games, and ask anyone who came up looking for a new game if they had played what I was thinking about getting. I would be stuck with that game for 4 months, so If I made a bad choice, oh well, to bad, so sad.

The times are changing I live WAY out in the country, you will need to drive down three different dirt/mud roads, after leaving the highways to get my house. I've used LTE internet for a very long time but yesterday there were trucks and tractors with backhoe's out by the road with a big orange wire spool. So I went out to be friendly, (Most would call it being nosy, I call it being friendly) They told me they were installing Fiber Optic lines for high speed internet. Can you believe that? Fast internet has came to the country, things are really changing now. I'm not going to understand how to act with this internet, mine gets 12-MBPS download and 2-MBPS upload and in three months I will have fiber optic, They told me the speed would be 5-gigs download and 5-gigs upload. WoW, So yes, I can see games going up in price. Soon games will be online only and you will need a new monthly sub for each game you are wanting to play.

Content:
Back in the 90s, prices like that were common because ROM carts were expensive to manufacture. The more expensive games used higher memory and graphic enhancement chips. Hence why games like Street Fighter Alpha 2 and Chrono Trigger were $70 as they were on 32Mb carts, second largest available on the SNES. 

The high price of carts is why so many publishers jumped to the PlayStation. CDs held insane amounts of data at barely a fraction of the cost. Switch carts are only slightly more expensive than a blu-ray. So there's no excuse for the price hike.

Author: @1023Bobby
Content:
I specifically remember on my 10th birthday, I purchased a physical copy of The Legand of Zelda. The price was $59.99.

Can anyone tell me a product that hasn't tripled in price since 1987? In today's money $170 would be the equivalent to $60 in 1987. Why are video games excluded from the overall average of how things change in price? 

It's sad that the world is fading from physical media. The Best Buy in my area no longer carries physical movies or music. I think games are obviously next. 

Everything is a service now. Video games will soon be a service too. We all understand that Xbox Gamepass is the equivalent to Netflix in regards to games. Soon all game companies will adapt to that subscription based service format. That will inevitably be followed by AAA studios and individual developers. 

My point is that people have multiple streaming services and on average spend $40 a month to have access. That's almost $500 a year. 

The keyword above is "access". You don't own anything. You're paying a fee for access that turn into memories. 

If a massive game like GTAV would have costed $300...I , like most, would still have purchased it. I also would have paid a reasonable price for monthly "access". Because I look at the exorbitant amount of hours I would play. 

Grand Theft Auto releases are usually some of the most beloved and expensive to create and offer an almost endless amount of entertainment. Majority speaking.... 

Some games will have 100's, sometimes 1000's of hours of content. Some games can be completed in 2 hours. I would not spend $300 for a yearly release title like COD, FIFA, NBA 2K. 

To wrap this up..... people sometimes forget how many aspects go into the final pricing of a product. The world is rapidly changing in all demographics. It's hard to process everything life gives each of us but the fact is, we are currently living and dealing with a digital world that grows by the second. At the end of the day, we will spend whatever something costs if we want it bad enough. It's all relative to the product and it's offering.
